33.0.0.en: As Jacob was walking with his wives and children, he saw Esau coming from afar with his four hundred men. He feared their great number, despite God's appearing to him and blessing him. So he divided those with him into three groups: the two maidservants, Bilhah and Zilpah, with their children in front, followed by Leah and her children, then the third group, which was Rachel and her son Joseph. As for himself, he went ahead of them all and bowed himself to the ground seven times as he drew near to Esau. This shows Jacob's feelings, which were:

33.0.1.en: 1- His love for Rachel, so he placed her at the end of the procession, so that if Esau attacked she would have a chance to escape, with Leah before her, to have a middle chance of escape, while the two maidservants were in front.

33.0.2.en: 2- He went ahead of them all, sacrificing himself, so that if Esau attacked he would be the first to die. In this he is a type of Christ the Redeemer, who dies for His Church.

33.0.3.en: 3- He bowed seven times, a complete number that signifies the work of the Holy Spirit in the believing person. This shows how humble Jacob was in abasing himself before Esau, and his respect and honor for him.

33.1.0.en: God worked in Esau's heart when he saw Jacob. Perhaps it reminded him of the days of their boyhood, their love, their play and their being together, and made him forget the cause of his anger, which was the stealing of his blessing. So his heart yearned toward his brother Jacob, and he ran quickly to meet him, embraced him and kissed him. Both were moved by this meeting of love after twenty years, and their tears flowed.

33.2.0.en: When Esau saw the women and children who were with Jacob, he asked him about them. Jacob told him that they were his wives and his children whom God had graciously given him. Then he presented each wife with her children, and they bowed before Esau. This shows the following:

33.2.1.en: 1- Jacob's sense that God alone is the source of all his blessings.

33.2.2.en: 2- That he took care to teach the members of his household humility in dealing with others, and respect for them.

33.3.0.en: Esau also asked his brother Jacob about the droves of flocks that had reached him before he saw him, and he called them an army because they were so many. Jacob answered that it was a small gift he presented to him so that he might be pleased with him. Esau said that he had many possessions, trying to return the gift to Jacob, who urged him to take it, and in the end he accepted.

33.4.0.en: After Esau had shown feelings of love in kissing and embracing his brother, and then in trying to return the gift to him, we find him offering his love again in proposing to accompany him to Canaan, where he lived, with Esau going ahead as his guide until he brought him to the place where he would settle. But Jacob excused himself, because he had small children with him, besides newly born animals; if he went quickly with all this company, they might not endure it and might faint on the way. So he asked leave for Esau to go ahead, and Jacob and those with him would come on slowly.

33.5.0.en: Esau's love appears for the fourth time in his offer to Jacob to leave with him some of his men to guide him on the way and guard him. But Jacob thanked him for this and declared his joy at the grace he had found in Esau's eyes, and assured him that he could go on by himself with those who were with him. So they bade each other farewell, and Esau went back to his place in Seir.

33.5.1.en: God is able to change the hearts of those who are hostile to you, so that they love you and are at peace with you, and even show concern for you. So be reassured, for you are not alone, and God is able to give you favor in the eyes of all. Seek Him and repeat His name, and you will feel His presence with you and rejoice in Him.

33.6.s.en: (2) Jacob's settling in the land of Canaan

33.6.0.en: Succoth: it means booths. There is a city of this name about a mile east of the Jordan, and another of the same name west of the Jordan, besides the one near Rameses in Egypt (Ex 12:37). Jacob went on his way southward and came to a place where he made booths for his cattle, so he called the name of the place Succoth, because he made booths there.

33.7.0.en: Shechem: a city lying west of the Jordan River between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, and now called Nablus.

33.7.1.en: Jacob journeyed until he came near a city called Shechem in the land of Canaan.

33.8.0.en: Kesitah: a metal coin stamped with the figure of a lamb, and of great value.

33.8.1.en: Jacob bought a parcel of ground near the city of Shechem, paying its price, which was a hundred pieces of money (kesitah), and pitched his tents and booths there. In this parcel the children of Israel buried the bones of Joseph when they came out of Egypt (Josh 24:32), and afterward they moved them to the cave of Machpelah.

33.9.0.en: The most important thing Jacob did after settling in Canaan was that he built an altar and offered sacrifices to God in the midst of the idolaters who were spread around him.

33.9.1.en: Thank God after every work you complete or every place you reach, to declare to yourself that your leader and the ruler of your life is God. Do not be preoccupied with the conduct of those around you, in their distance from God and their preoccupation with the world, for your distinction and your strength lie in God's being with you, so you enjoy His blessings and rejoice in His presence within you.

34.0.0.en: After Jacob settled near the city of Shechem, his daughter Dinah went out to get to know the daughters of the pagan tribe living near them, out of curiosity to learn their customs and to mix with them, though she knew they were wicked and far from God.

34.1.1.en: Shechem: the prince of the tribe in this city, son of Hamor, the chief of the tribe, which was one of the Hivite tribes. Shechem saw Dinah walking in the city and was taken with her beauty. He spoke with her and was able to lure her until he lay with her and raped her.

34.1.2.en: Control your curiosity to know the news of evil and the events of the world, which can make you stumble. Do not give yourself over to the media without restraint, lest you expose yourself to falling into sin, and Satan humbles you and robs you of your purity, trying to lead you away from God.

34.2.s.en: (2) Hamor asks for Dinah as a wife for Shechem

34.2.0.en: Shechem continued in his love for Dinah, with whom he had committed fornication; indeed his heart clung to her and he wanted to marry her, so he asked his father to get her for him as a wife.

34.3.0.en: Jacob learned what had happened to his daughter. Perhaps she remained with Shechem after he raped her, until Hamor came, on the same day or after it, to ask her father for her hand; or perhaps she kept going out to meet him for several days and then stayed with him, and then Hamor came to seek her for his son from her father. In any case, Jacob was greatly grieved, and from the horror of the calamity he kept silent and waited until his sons came from their work tending the flock, so that he might consult with them.

34.4.0.en: Hamor decided to seek Dinah for his son Shechem, so he took him with him and visited Jacob and asked him for Dinah to be Shechem's wife.

34.5.0.en: During the visit of Hamor and Shechem to Jacob to seek Dinah's hand, Jacob's sons arrived after finishing their work in the pasture, and they heard and learned the whole story. They were very angry at Shechem's rape of their sister Dinah, and at how such a vile thing had happened in the family of their father Israel, which was distinguished by purity, righteousness and a clean life with God. This matter was not merely unseemly but a great calamity that no one had expected.

34.6.0.en: Hamor tried to resolve the problem and ease her brothers' anger by proposing that this marriage be the beginning of good relations between the family of Israel and their tribe, so that they would unite in one life, trade together, and have one land between them. For Israel was a stranger in the land, and he would regard this treaty and intermarriage as a kind of security for him.

34.7.0.en: Shechem the son of Hamor made another offer showing his love for Dinah and his attachment to her. He asked Jacob and his sons to set the dowry, that is, what is paid to the bride, and the gift presented to her family, as they saw fit; indeed they should multiply it and ask for the greatest dowry and gift, and he and his father were ready to meet their demands.

34.7.1.en: Do not be hasty in your actions, lest you fall into sins that cannot be resolved and wrong others, so that they do not forgive you however much you try to settle it. Control your tongue and your actions, pray before you undertake anything, and always keep the fear of God before your eyes, so that you do not sin against Him or wrong anyone.

34.8.s.en: (3) The deceitful speech of Jacob's sons

34.8.0.en: In their distress over what had happened, Jacob's sons thought of a deception in order to take revenge on the tribe of Shechem and not on Shechem alone.

34.9.0.en: Jacob's sons pretended to agree to Dinah's marriage to Shechem, but they told Hamor and his son that it was their custom that every male be circumcised, and that they could not intermarry with any foreign tribe unless all its males were circumcised. So if they wanted Dinah to marry Shechem, all the males of their tribe must be circumcised.

34.10.0.en: Then they said to Hamor and his son that if they would not consent to be circumcised, they would take Dinah and go to their tents. This shows that Dinah had remained with Shechem after he raped her, whether on the same day or some days later.

34.10.1.en: Here it appears that Jacob's sons, led by Simeon and Levi, used religion as a deception to reach their evil ends. This is a very wrong thing, that is, to pretend to be religious in order to accomplish evil.

34.10.2.en: Know that your spiritual practices are a private matter between you and God; indeed Christ commands you to keep them in secret. So do not try to display these practices before people, or to use them for any personal ends in your dealings with all those around you, or to hide some of your sins.

34.11.s.en: (4) Hamor and Shechem's speech to the men of their city

34.11.0.en: Shechem and his father agreed to the condition Jacob's sons asked, which was the circumcision of every male, and they left their presence to carry out the matter. Shechem was like a prince in his tribe and held a great position, and therefore what he and his father said had an influence on the whole tribe.

34.12.0.en: The gate of their city: the square where the people gather.

34.12.1.en: Hamor and his son Shechem stood at the entrance of their city and spoke to the crowds of the people. They told them that Jacob and his clan were peaceable people, and that they could ally themselves with them and intermarry with them and share life with them, but there was one condition: that all the males be circumcised, so that they might all live as one family. One of the benefits of this intermarriage between the two tribes was that the others' possessions would become theirs, that is, the possessions of the tribe of Shechem, since they would become one great people with many possessions. All this was to encourage them to accept the matter.

34.13.0.en: All who went out of the gate of his city: all the working men of the city who go out to their work.

34.13.1.en: Because of the standing of Hamor and Shechem among the people, and because the offer was beneficial and convincing, the people of the city agreed to circumcision in order to intermarry with the family of Israel, and they were circumcised.

34.13.2.en: Present your words to others in a convincing way so that they accept them, and care for their feelings and opinions; for in proportion as you respect people's opinions they respect yours and understand you, and even love your company and companionship.

34.14.s.en: (5) The killing of the men of Shechem's tribe

34.14.1.en: Simeon and Levi led a band made up of their servants and attacked the city of Shechem and killed all its men, including Shechem and Hamor. No one resisted them because of the pain of their circumcision, for they attacked on the third day after being circumcised. And they took their sister Dinah, who was in Shechem's house.

34.15.0.en: The rest of Jacob's sons also attacked the city of Shechem after the men were killed, and joined the killers in plundering their spoil and taking captive their women and children to be servants and slaves for them. Thus they brought this tribe to an end.

34.16.0.en: Jacob was greatly distressed at what had happened, because it was an unjust revenge. Instead of refusing the marriage or punishing Shechem with some penalty, they killed innocent men, took captive their women and children, and plundered their spoil. This was a terrible injustice. On the other hand, he feared that the neighboring tribes, when they heard what had happened, would rise against him and kill him, especially since his clan was few in number compared with the large tribes around them.

34.17.0.en: Simeon and Levi justified their crime by saying that they could not keep silent over the rape of their sister Dinah and her being treated as a harlot.

34.17.1.en: Do not be rash in your anger and make unwise decisions, but wait, think and pray first, that God may guide you and you may do His will; then you will not regret it because of God's anger against you and the anger of people as well.

35.0.0.en: Jacob was troubled after his sons killed the tribe of Shechem, so God intervened to rescue him and restore his peace. He commanded him to move to Bethel, where God had appeared to him at the ladder when he was fleeing from Esau (ch. 28:10-22). This was the place where he vowed that God would have a house and he would worship Him. He had not gone there immediately after coming from Padan-aram, from his uncle Laban, and perhaps this was by divine arrangement so that he might dwell in different places in the land of Canaan, for God to prove to him that all the land of Canaan would be his and his offspring's.

35.1.0.en: Jacob prepared to depart for Bethel in obedience to God's commands, and told those with him to prepare in two ways:

35.1.1.en: 1- Putting away the strange gods and getting rid of them. These were the small images of the pagan gods that people anciently used for good omens or to seek help. They were either the images Rachel had taken from her father and had not yet got rid of, or some images his servants may have kept during their stay in Padan-aram. This was to sanctify the heart and life for the worship of God.

35.1.2.en: 2- Changing their garments and putting on new, clean clothes as a symbol of purity and cleanness of heart.

35.2.0.en: Jacob declared to those with him that this preparation was not only for moving to another place but for a holy place for the worship of God, where he would build an altar and thank God who had kept him on his way and brought him back to Bethel, and so fulfill what he had promised God in this place.

35.3.0.en: All who were with Jacob obeyed his words, and they gave him not only the images of the pagan gods but also the gold earrings they wore in their ears, because they were of the kind used in the worship of idols, since they bore the engraving of the gods. He took them all and hid them under an oak (terebinth) tree at Shechem, where they were dwelling.

35.3.1.en: If you want to worship God, you must rid yourself of your old sins through repentance, and of all the material attachments that control you, so that your heart is free for God, and you use the world only to meet your needs, and your aim is to enjoy fellowship with God.

35.4.0.en: The procession of Jacob and his family moved from Shechem toward Bethel, and God gave them awe and fear in the eyes of all their neighboring tribes, so that none of them harmed them because of what they had done to the tribe of Shechem.

35.4.1.en: If you please God and obey His commandments, He gives you favor in the eyes of those around you, so they do not harm you even if you have hidden or visible sins, for God covers you because of your repentance and your taking refuge in Him.

35.5.0.en: Jacob came to the city of Luz, which was afterward called Bethel, and built an altar to God and offered sacrifices of thanksgiving to God, who had kept him on his journey to Padan-aram and brought him back to this holy place.

35.6.0.en: Beneath Bethel: a low place in Bethel.

35.6.1.en: Allon-bachuth: that is, the oak of weeping.

35.6.2.en: Jacob used to visit his father Isaac, and Rebekah had most likely died, since she is not mentioned after his return from his uncle Laban. So he asked his father's leave and took Rebekah's nurse, who was called Deborah, to live with him as a consolation for the mother of whom he had been deprived. When they reached Bethel and had given thanks to God, Deborah died, and they buried her in a low place in Bethel under one of the trees, and wept much for her, because in that generation they honored nurses and gave them a position like that of mothers. This signifies care for those who bring up others in the Church of God, and care also for those who have departed, because Bethel, the house of God, gathers together the teachers and the children, the departed and the living. Perhaps this is the reason for mentioning Deborah's burial and the attention given to it: that the Church cares for teachers and shepherds and honors them in appreciation of their labors.

35.7.0.en: Since Jacob obeyed God and moved to Bethel, rid himself of the idols, purified himself and those with him, and then offered thanksgiving and sacrifices, God appeared to him and blessed him and confirmed to him the change of his name to Israel, that is, one who wrestles with God, so that he might begin a new, holy life with Him.

35.8.0.en: God confirmed to him the promise that his offspring would become great, and that nations would come from him and kings from his offspring would reign over them. This is what happened in the twelve tribes and the kings who reigned, such as David and Solomon.

35.9.0.en: He also promised him the inheritance of the Promised Land, that is, Canaan, as He had promised his fathers, and it is a type of the Kingdom of Heaven. Then God went up to heaven and disappeared from him.

35.10.0.en: Jacob rejoiced greatly at God's appearing to him, so he set up a pillar testifying to God's appearing to him and poured oil on it, which signifies the dedication and consecration of the place for the worship of God. He also poured out wine, which signifies joy in the worship of God and fellowship with Him. And he called the place Bethel, because God appeared there twice: the first in the dream of the ladder (ch. 28:12) and the second now in speaking with him.

35.11.s.en: (2) The death of Rachel and the birth of Benjamin

35.11.0.en: Ephrath: it means fruitful land, and it later became Bethlehem, that is, the house of bread, where Christ was born, and it is six miles south of Jerusalem.

35.11.1.en: God graciously granted Rachel conception a second time. After they had spent a period in Bethel they moved on, seeking pasture for the flocks, and because God had assured him that he would inherit all the land of Canaan. On their way to the city of Ephrath, and a mile from it, Rachel felt the pains of childbirth, and her labor was hard and her pains severe.

35.12.0.en: Rachel suffered greatly in her labor, and the midwife who was helping her tried to cheer and reassure her that she would bear a son, as she had wished from God at the birth of Joseph, that He would add to her another son.

35.13.0.en: Ben-oni: it means son of sorrow.

35.13.1.en: Benjamin: it means son of the right hand, that is, of strength, joy and blessing.

35.13.2.en: Rachel felt that she was nearing death from the severity of the pain, so she called her son's name Ben-oni because of her great sorrow and pains, and then she died. But his father Jacob called his name Benjamin.

35.14.0.en: Rachel died and they buried her on the way to Ephrath, and Jacob set up a pillar on her grave to honor her, because he loved her very much. This pillar remained until this day, that is, the day Moses wrote the book, and indeed traces of this tomb are still found in Bethlehem.

35.14.1.en: Death and life are mingled together. So rejoice in every new day God gives you, and use it to prepare for the Kingdom of Heaven. That is, rejoice at the beginning of the day and remember death, and you will live above the world, enjoying fellowship with God.

35.15.0.en: Migdal Eder: the tower of the flock, which lies a mile east of Bethlehem.

35.15.1.en: Israel continued his journeys with his family, and came to Migdal Eder and pitched his tents there.

35.16.0.en: After Rachel's death, Reuben, the eldest of Israel's sons, dared to look upon Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant and his father's concubine, and desired her and lay with her. This is a great sin that neither custom nor the traditions of his time allowed, and lust was his only motive for wronging God and his father; and when Israel heard of it he was greatly grieved. Thus Reuben lost his birthright, and Joseph took it, who lived a more righteous life than the rest of his brothers, and God gave him a double portion, that is, more than the rest of his brothers (1 Chr 5:1-2).

35.16.1.en: Be in control of your desires, whether of the eye, the thought or inward longings, and drive them away by repeating the Psalms and prostrating before God, so that they do not dominate you and you fall into evil deeds and anger God. Even if you fall, hasten to repentance and to guarding your senses and thoughts, for God still loves you and is ready to rescue you from every evil.

35.17.0.en: Here is given a list of the names of the twelve sons of Israel who were born to him of his two wives and two concubines in Padan-aram. He means here that most of them, the eleven, were born at Laban's, while the last, Benjamin, was born in Canaan.
